summary:
Section 210 of the Penal Code criminalises male same-sex sexual activity. Anal or oral sex, whether between two men or between a man and a woman, is punishable as sodomy with up to fourteen years' imprisonment; other same-sex acts carry up to three years. Sex between women is not restricted by law. The penalties attach to sexual acts rather than to transgender identity as such.

As of 2024 Papua New Guinea has no legal recognition of transgender or gender-diverse identities. The sources state no transgender-specific criminal provision, identity-document rule, screening procedure, facilities rule, custody rule or healthcare restriction of any kind, so neither a documented legal exposure nor a documented legal protection specific to gender identity is available to a trans visitor.

Enforcement is sporadic. No prosecutions directed at LGBTQ people were recorded in 2012. In 2015 a man charged with indecent acts between males pleaded guilty and received a suspended sentence with community service and mandatory counselling; in 2022 two men were arrested after having sex. Decriminalisation was described as not a priority in 2011, and in 2023 the government confirmed it did not intend to repeal the laws criminalising male homosexuality, holding that existing provisions against violence and abuse were sufficient.

Police are documented as a direct source of violence. A 2011 study identified police as one of the main sources of violence against men who have sex with men and against transgender people. Reporting from Port Moresby describes gay men sexually abused, raped and beaten by officers, with abuse commonly continuing after a report is made because the victim is treated as the perpetrator.

Violence against LGBTQ people is reported across the country, including in Port Moresby, and has driven many people to relocate to Hanuabada village on the capital's outskirts. Residents there live openly; in 2014 transgender residents were reported wearing women's clothing in the street without retaliation, and the village is described as a sanctuary for the local LGBTQ community. Outside it, a 24-year-old gay man recounted being pelted with stones and bottles.

The words lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender carry heavy stigma, and LGBTQ people report discrimination in daily life and difficulty finding employment. Public views are mixed and homophobia is widespread; the sources describe homosexuality as more accepted in coastal areas than in the Highlands, a statement about LGBTQ people generally rather than about transgender people specifically.
tangentialFactors:
The Asian Development Bank's publication 'Assessment of the Legal Status of Sexual and Gender Minorities in 17 Countries in Asia and the Pacific', content dated 17 May 2024, lists Papua New Guinea among the seventeen assessed countries, with decriminalization and SOGIESC inclusion among its keywords. The publication's country-level findings are not reproduced in this inventory.

The accountability climate for violence generally is weak, which shapes what a visitor can expect if an assault is reported. Human Rights Commentary of 27 January 2009 records a mob stripping, beating with hot iron rods and burning a woman accused of sorcery within yards of a police station; provincial commanders recorded more than fifty sorcery-related killings in two highlands provinces in 2008, with perpetrators rarely brought to justice; sorcery accusations, sometimes linked to HIV deaths, were used to conceal murders and mitigate sentences; and police routinely took no action.

Human Rights Watch's 2017 world report assessment, reported on 13 January 2017, found that the government had failed to protect women and children and to respond to corruption and police violence, and that police abuse, including of children, continued to be reported with little accountability even for fatalities or egregious physical abuse.

Hanuabada functions as a single documented pocket of tolerance rather than evidence of national conditions. It is described as a village built over the sea where the gay community is accepted, set against a national picture in which sex between men is illegal and stigma and violence are widespread; campaigners quoted there say attitudes shift with exposure to the LGBT community.
localsOnly:
Transgender Papua New Guineans use the Tok Pisin word palopa, reportedly derived from the name of the American singer Jennifer Lopez, to refer to a cultural and traditional third gender. The Sambia recognise a traditional third gender called kwolu-aatmwol, literally 'male thing transforming into female thing'. These are indigenous categories with no legal standing attached.

Residents face the absence of legal recognition directly: there is no mechanism in the sources for changing gender markers on identity documents, and LGBTQ people report discrimination in daily life and struggle to find jobs. Employment and documentation effects fall on residents rather than visitors.

Hanuabada village on the outskirts of Port Moresby is described as a gay village and a sanctuary for local LGBTQ people, and as a destination for those fleeing rape and violence elsewhere in the country. It is one documented community, not a national pattern.
outOfScopeNotes:
No transgender-specific rule on identity documents, airport or police screening, bathroom or other facilities, detention or custody, or access to gender-affirming healthcare is stated anywhere in the inventory. Whether such rules exist and what they say is unresolved and not sourced here.

No trans-specific violence figure with a denominator, a measurement period or a comparison to the general homicide rate appears in the inventory, so no trans-specific rate can be stated. The documented incidents are individual accounts from 2014 and undated reporting, and the most recent enforcement actions in the record are from 2015 and 2022; no later instance is documented.

The 2015 and 2022 enforcement cases concern men charged over sex with men; no case in the inventory involves a transgender defendant, so how the sodomy provisions would be applied to a trans person is unresolved.

The coastal-versus-Highlands acceptance contrast is stated for LGBTQ people generally. No documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically appears in the sources, so that contrast cannot be read as trans-specific.

The Asian Development Bank publication is cited only for its listing of Papua New Guinea; its substantive country assessment is not available in this inventory.
